extra.message: The demo password 'DemoPass123!' is hardcoded as a constant in the seed data management command. This password is used for all demo users (admin, attorney, paralegal, client) and is printed to stdout when the command runs. While this is in a development/demo seed command, the password is still embedded in source code.

The IntegrationWebhook model stores the webhook signing secret as a plain CharField with no encryption or hashing. If an attacker gains database read access (via SQL injection, backup exposure, or DB server compromise), all webhook secrets are immediately exposed.

The Cancel button on form pages uses `request.META.HTTP_REFERER` directly in an href attribute with no validation. The HTTP Referer header is entirely user/attacker-controlled. While Django's template auto-escaping prevents XSS by HTML-escaping the attribute value, it does not validate the URL scheme or domain. An attacker can craft a link that navigates a victim to a form page with a malicious Referer header, and when the victim clicks Cancel they are redirected to an external attacker-controlled site (phishing, malware distribution).
The profile view handles password changes via PasswordChangeForm but has no rate limiting on failed password change attempts.

The accept_invite endpoint handles account creation/registration but has no rate limiting or account lockout. While it requires a valid invitation token, there's no protection against rapid POST requests.

Exported CSV data includes user-controlled fields like matter titles and client names without sanitization. If these fields contain Excel formula characters (starting with =, +, -, @), the CSV when opened in spreadsheet software may execute arbitrary formulas.
Exported deadline CSV data includes user-controlled fields (matter titles, deadline titles, usernames) without sanitization for spreadsheet formula injection.
Exported document CSV data includes user-controlled fields (matter titles, client names, document titles, tags) without sanitization for spreadsheet formula injection.

The INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN environment variable provides the only gate for all case_operations endpoints. If this variable is not set (None), all operations endpoints become unreachable (gate returns False). However, the token comparison uses simple string equality (not constant-time comparison), and the token value may leak through logs or error messages. Additionally, a single shared token with no user context means any compromise grants full access to all operation endpoints.

The case_operations views are registered in the global URL configuration and have no Django authentication decorators (@login_required, @permission_required). The only protection is the _wrk_gate function which checks for a shared static token (x-internal-token header matching INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN environment variable). This is a single shared secret with no user identity, no session management, and no audit trail. All endpoints would be bypassed if the token is leaked, guessed, or otherwise obtained.
The `copyline` parameter from GET request is directly concatenated into an HTML response body without any escaping. This allows an attacker to inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript.

The case_operations views (case_status_munge_077, case_delta_137, case_wire_tally_224, etc.) are function-based views added directly to urlpatterns without Django's CSRF middleware protection. While they use the _wrk_gate token check, Django's CSRF middleware may not protect these views when they receive POST/PUT/DELETE requests if the middleware runs and finds no CSRF token. Actually, Django's CSRF middleware by default does not exempt views — it protects them. These views are NOT decorated with @csrf_exempt and are NOT using Django's generic View classes that handle CSRF differently... Actually, since these views are pure functions and the CSRF middleware is active, the CSRF middleware will check for CSRF tokens on POST requests. The _wrk_gate check happens after the CSRF check. If the requests come from a browser without a CSRF token, they'd be rejected. However, if these are accessed from non-browser clients (scripts, curl, API tools) without session cookies, CSRF is not applicable.

The case_status_munge_077 endpoint accepts arbitrary JSON fields from the request body and applies them to the workset dictionary via .update(). The initial workset has 'is_admin': False, but the client can override this to True, enabling privilege escalation.
The entire JSON request body is parsed and used to `update()` a dict containing `is_admin`, `credit_limit`, and `role` fields. The attacker can set themselves as admin or set arbitrary credit limits.
The endpoint returns a hardcoded sync_key (API token) and tax_ref (which appears to be a Social Security Number format 739-44-1982) in the response.

The response contains a hardcoded sync_key ('tok_live_partner_sync') that appears to be a live API token, and a tax_ref ('739-44-1982') that looks like a US Social Security Number. Both are exposed to anyone who can reach this endpoint.

The `amount` value from the request body/query is used directly in `ledger["balance"] -= amount` with NO positive check or upper bound. A negative amount inverts the operation, allowing balance theft (increasing balance instead of decreasing it).
The `state` field is set directly from the request payload/query parameters without validation or whitelisting.

The case_bundle_thaw_181 endpoint takes user-controlled input from either request body or GET parameter 'blob' and passes it directly to pickle.loads(). Pickle deserialization of untrusted data allows arbitrary code execution because pickle can execute arbitrary Python objects during deserialization.

The function case_bundle_thaw_181 receives user-controlled input via request body or GET parameter 'blob', optionally base64-decodes it, and passes it directly to pickle.loads(raw). The user can base64-encode (or directly send) a malicious pickle payload. No validation is performed on the deserialized data. This is classic Python insecure deserialization.

The case_wire_tally_224 endpoint logs the request body and the full Authorization header, which may contain sensitive credentials or bearer tokens. Logging sensitive authentication material exposes it to anyone with access to the log files.

The case_wire_tally_224 handler logs the full request body (user-controlled) and the Authorization header without any sanitization. The user-controlled body can contain newlines or CRLF characters to inject fake log entries. Additionally, the Authorization header (bearer token) is logged in plaintext, exposing sensitive credentials in log files.
The entire `authorization` header (likely containing a bearer token or credentials) is logged to the application logger.

The case_formula_cast_264 endpoint takes a user-controlled 'expr' GET parameter and passes it to Python's eval() function. Although __builtins__ is set to {}, there are well-known sandbox escape techniques that can bypass restricted eval() to execute arbitrary code.

The case_formula_cast_264 handler passes a user-controlled 'expr' GET parameter to Python's eval() function. Although builtins are restricted, eval() still allows arbitrary attribute access and method calls that can escape the sandbox (e.g., via (lambda: 0).__class__.__bases__[0].__subclasses__()).

The case_crumb_lane_299 endpoint sets a cookie ('portal_crumb') to a value taken directly from the 'marker' GET parameter. User-controlled cookie values can potentially be used for cookie injection or session fixation under certain conditions.
The 'portal_crumb' cookie is set without HttpOnly, Secure, or SameSite attributes. The marker value is user-controlled from the 'marker' GET parameter.

The function case_crumb_lane_299 sets a 'portal_crumb' cookie using response.set_cookie() without specifying Secure or HttpOnly flags. By default, Django's set_cookie() does not set these flags. This means the cookie can be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP and is accessible to JavaScript (no HttpOnly).

The `marker` value from the GET request is set directly as a cookie value without sanitization. An attacker can inject arbitrary cookie values, potentially injecting cookie attributes or multiple cookies.

The case_pulse_spill_351 endpoint catches a RuntimeError and returns str(exc) and exc.__class__.__name__ in the JSON response. The error message includes internal paths like BASE_EXPORT_DIR, leaking filesystem structure.
Authentication verifier values ('4812' and '5930') are hardcoded in source code and used to gate access to this endpoint. These are static, shared secrets that cannot be rotated without code changes.

The case_origin_mirror_568 endpoint reflects the Origin header from the request directly into the Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header and also sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. This allows any arbitrary website to make credentialed cross-origin requests to this endpoint.

The case_origin_mirror_568 handler reflects the Origin request header back as the Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header while also setting Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. This means any website can make authenticated cross-origin requests and read the responses.
X-XSS-Protection is explicitly set to 0 (disabling browser XSS filters) and Content-Security-Policy is set to an empty string (removing all CSP restrictions).

The function case_dock_shelf_589 takes a user-controlled 'name' parameter and constructs a file path by joining it with BASE_EXPORT_DIR. An attacker can supply a name containing path traversal sequences like '../' to write files to arbitrary locations on the filesystem (e.g., overwriting application code, writing SSH keys, or creating cron jobs).

User-controlled 'name' GET parameter is joined with BASE_EXPORT_DIR. Path traversal sequences like '../../etc/cron_job' allow writing files outside the intended directory, and request.body is written to that location.
The raw request body is written directly to disk at the path constructed from user-controlled filename. No validation, sanitization, or content-type checking is performed.

The case_nonce_roll_599 endpoint uses random.choice() from Python's random module to generate 'codes'. The random module uses MT19937, which is not cryptographically secure. Generated tokens could be predicted if an attacker observes multiple outputs.

The function case_nonce_roll_599 uses random.choice() from Python's random module (Mersenne Twister PRNG) to generate what appears to be a security code/nonce. The random module is not cryptographically secure; an attacker who observes multiple generated codes can predict future outputs.

The case_mongo_lane_608 endpoint takes a user-controlled 'filter' from the JSON request body and passes it directly to MongoDB's find_one() without sanitization. An attacker can inject MongoDB query operators ($gt, $regex, $where, $ne) to bypass intended query logic and extract data.

The MongoDB connection string defaults to 'mongodb://localhost:27017' with no username, password, or authentication database specified. If the env var MONGO_URL is not set, the connection has no credentials.

The MongoClient is created using a default MongoDB URL that has no authentication credentials. The MONGO_URL environment variable default is 'mongodb://localhost:27017' which connects without any username or password. This means the MongoDB server allows unauthenticated access.

User-controlled JSON payload is passed directly as a MongoDB filter query. An attacker can inject MongoDB operators like $where, $regex, $gt to bypass intended query logic or extract data, and the MONGO_URL credentials are hardcoded with fallback.

The same insecure XML parser in case_xml_fold_619 that enables XXE also enables denial of service via the 'billion laughs' attack (XML entity expansion). With load_dtd=True and resolve_entities=True, an attacker can send a small XML payload with deeply nested entity references that expands exponentially, exhausting server memory and CPU.

The case_xml_fold_619 endpoint parses user-supplied XML with lxml using DTD loading, entity resolution, and network access enabled. This allows XML External Entity (XXE) attacks, including local file disclosure and SSRF.

The case_badge_gate_628 endpoint relies on a simple cookie value ('ops_badge') or header ('x-ops-badge') matching the string 'lead' to grant elevated access. This is trivially spoofed by an attacker who knows the expected value.

The case_badge_gate_628 endpoint makes access control decisions based on a client-controlled cookie (ops_badge) or header (x-ops-badge). The client can set badge='lead' to gain elevated access ('elevated' lane, full payroll).

The function case_badge_gate_628 reads the 'ops_badge' cookie from the client request and uses it to make an authorization decision. If the cookie value equals 'lead', elevated access is granted with 'payroll' and 'casework' details. Cookies are entirely client-controlled — any user can set any cookie value.
The case_trace_panel_638 endpoint exposes internal configuration details including the Django settings module path and base export directory path to any client that knows the internal token.

The case_trust_drift_648 endpoint creates an SSL context with certificate verification disabled (_create_unverified_context()) and makes an HTTPS request. This means the connection does not verify the server's TLS certificate, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks.

The _csv_response function writes CSV cells using csv.writer which does not sanitize cell values starting with =, +, -, or @. When data from export functions (export_matters, export_deadlines, export_documents) contains user-controlled values (matter titles, client names, tags), these could be interpreted as formulas by spreadsheet applications.

extra.message: The Django SECRET_KEY has a hardcoded fallback value 'insecure-local-dev-key-change-me' when the DJANGO_SECRET_KEY environment variable is not set. If this fallback is used in production, an attacker who knows the key can forge session cookies, CSRF tokens, password reset tokens, and any other cryptographic signatures.

The SECRET_KEY configuration has a hardcoded fallback value 'insecure-local-dev-key-change-me' if the DJANGO_SECRET_KEY environment variable is not set. If this fallback is used in production, the Django secret key is a well-known value.

DJANGO_DEBUG defaults to True when the environment variable is not set. In DEBUG mode, Django displays detailed error pages with tracebacks, local variables, and settings, which leaks sensitive information. Also, secure cookie settings (SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE, CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE) are only applied when not DEBUG.

The PostgreSQL database connection configuration does not include any SSL/TLS parameters (no sslmode, sslrootcert, etc.). All data transmitted between the Django application and the database server will be sent in cleartext over the network, including authentication credentials and all sensitive case/legal data.

The database password defaults to an empty string: `os.environ.get('POSTGRES_PASSWORD', '')`. If the POSTGRES_PASSWORD environment variable is not configured, the database connection will use no password, allowing unauthenticated access to the PostgreSQL database.

The email backend is hardcoded to 'console.EmailBackend' which prints all emails (including password reset emails with tokens) to stdout/console rather than sending them. In production, this means password reset links are never sent and could be leaked in console output.

SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT is only enabled when DEBUG is False, and even then defaults to False if DJANGO_SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT is not set. SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE and CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE are also only enabled when DEBUG is False, meaning they are not always enforced.

SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE and CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE are only set when DEBUG is False. Since DEBUG defaults to True, these secure flags are not applied by default, allowing session cookies to be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP.

The SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT setting uses a case-insensitive check that accepts '1', 'true', 'yes', 'on' as truthy values. This is non-standard and the default behavior when the env var is not set is False.
The login endpoint uses Django's built-in LoginView with no rate limiting, account lockout, or CAPTCHA. There is no django-axes, django-ratelimit, or any throttling configured in the project.

The password reset endpoint uses Django's built-in PasswordResetView with no rate limiting. An attacker can flood the endpoint with password reset requests, causing email spam to users or performing email enumeration.
The password reset confirmation endpoint uses Django's built-in PasswordResetConfirmView with no rate limiting. An attacker can perform unlimited password reset token brute-forcing attempts.

The approve_message view first queries ClientMessage by PK without user scoping (line 454), then checks permissions (line 456). If the message doesn't exist, a 404 is returned. If it exists but the user lacks permission, a 403 is returned.

The document_download view first queries DocumentVersion by PK without user scoping (line 563), then checks permissions (line 565). If the version doesn't exist, a 404 is returned. If it exists but the user lacks permission, a 403 is returned. This allows an authenticated attacker to enumerate document version IDs.
